Beállítom Biztos megélhetés nélkül nincs élhető magyar vidék, ezért is fontosak az olyan beruházások, mint a Nestlé Hungária Kft. új gyáregységei – mondta Magyar Péter miniszterelnök pénteken, a Nestlé Purina új gyártóüzemeinek, illetve egy automatizált magasraktárának átadásán. A büki állateledel-gyár új egységeinek átadóján az is elhangzott, hogy a beruházással 1800-ra nőtt az üzemben dolgozók száma. A Nestlé 1998-ban vásárolta meg a büki állateledelgyárat, amelynek fejlesztésére azóta összesen 325 milliárd forintot fordított. A gyár éves termelési kapacitása mostanra elérheti akár az 500 ezer tonnát is. A Nestlé egyik legnagyobb európai állateledel-gyárának számító büki üzemben a termékek kb. 95 százaléka exportra készül, és közel 50 országba jutnak el Magyarországról. Magyar Péter miniszterelnök beszédében kitért rá: fontos, hogy a munkaalapú társadalomtól a tudásalapú társadalom felé mozduljunk el. „Ezekben a gyáregységekben a robotika és az AI használata mindennapos, a technológia kiegészíti az itt dolgozók munkáját. A duális szakképzésben való részvétel pedig elősegíti, hogy minél több fiatal szerezhessen gyakorlati tapasztalatot a terepen, hogy olyan, rugalmas tudással bíró szakemberekké váljanak, akik a gyorsan változó világban később is megtalálják a helyüket. A tudásba való befektetés a legbiztosabb befektetés, amelyet egy nemzet tehet.” A Nestlé a sajtóközleményében azt írja, hogy a cég a magyarországi működésével a hazai GDP mintegy fél százalékához járul hozzá. A cég közvetlen gazdasági hatása mellett ugyanis beszállítóin és kereskedelmi partnerein, valamint saját és beszállítói munkatársai fogyasztásán keresztül is növeli a gazdaság teljesítményét. A Nestlé magyarországi jelenléte így összesen 22 100 munkahely létét támogatja. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Home affairs minister Tony Burke says the new rules to ‘put an end to student visa hopping’ are about ‘ensuring we have a migration system that Australians can be confident in’. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Home affairs minister Tony Burke says the new rules to ‘put an end to student visa hopping’ are about ‘ensuring we have a migration system that Australians can be confident in’. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Australian immigration and asylum Labor targets ‘visa hopping’ international students in crackdown on ‘permanently temporary’ migration Migration agents and lawyers ‘selling false hope’ to people seeking to stay in Australia also in ministers’ sights as they seek to reduce overseas arrivals Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Krishani Dhanji Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.33 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 22.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Visa hopping” international students, migration agents and lawyers trying to “game” the migration system will be targeted by the federal government, as Labor unveils a further crackdown. The changes announced on Friday mean international students will soon need to apply for a separate visa to transfer courses, on top of previously announced rules that prevent transferring to a lower grade course, such as switching from a bachelor’s or masters’ degree to a vocational program. In a speech to the Migration Institute of Australia, the assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said the changes would stop the increase of “permanently temporary” migration. “When Australians go to another country they do not believe they have some God-given right to hop around from visa to visa for years or decades and game other nations’ appeals and courts systems – and neither should guests in our country,” Hill said. In a social media post, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke , said: “As of today there are new rules to put an end to student visa hopping. It’s all about ensuring we have a migration system that Australians can be confident in.” The changes are part of a broader reform package to lower net overseas migration but the government has been forced to amend rules without separate legislation, because it does not have the support of the Coalition or the Greens. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Labor wants to bring net overseas migration down from its annual level of almost 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028. Separately, there are now more than 400,000 people on bridging visas, temporary visas that can be issued if a visa expires and someone is waiting for a decision on their next application, or to asylum seekers and non-citizens. A large cohort of these can be international students applying for a different visa – the government is trying to bring this number down. Australian colleges warned ‘do not try to game’ student visas after last-minute enrolments for cancelled diploma soar Read more Hill said from 1 July 2027 a student’s visa will not be extended even if they are transferring into a different course, to prevent “rorting and ensures students can’t just not turn up for the first 6 months, fail their subjects then go to a cheaper provider”. In the interim, a student will not be able to transfer within 12 months of beginning a course. Migration agents and lawyers selling “false hope” by helping individuals to pursue baseless visa claims to help them stay in Australia longer will also be targeted under new rules. The government is proposing changes to ban migration agents assisting with an application “they know, or reasonably ought to know, does not have a reasonable factual or legal basis”. skip past promotion Hill said the Department of Home Affairs would consult on how to ensure migration lawyers are also held to account for similar poor practices. “Increasingly sophisticated forms of migration-related misconduct and a small number of bad actors cause disproportionate harm, often targeting people at vulnerable points in their lives when they are highly susceptible to misleading claims, false promises and unrealistic assurances,” Hill said. “Taking cash in those circumstances is not helping people – it’s exploiting them and selling false hope.” Hill said one lawyer had submitted an application with the intention of it being refused, it being appealed to the administrative appeals tribunal to be refused again and then ultimately being submitted for a ministerial intervention. “We have also seen some pretty outrageous online advertising by lawyers,” he said. “Ads that appear to coach people on how to claim they’re bisexual when they’re not, or how to convince the department they’re being persecuted when they’re not, in order to support a protection claim. “The current system for lawyers authorises and arguably requires them to act for clients in ways that damage the administration of and public confidence in Australia’s migration system.” Explore more on these topics Australian immigration and asylum Australian politics Australian universities https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text: Image source, TV3 Image caption, It is illegal to misuse Ghana's cedi, including by defacing or unlawfully altering banknotes By Thomas Naadi BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Accra Published 6 October 2026 Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes. The Bank of Ghana says the practice is illegal and amounts to misuse and improper handling of the cedi, the national currency. The arrests, carried out in collaboration with the police, followed a tip-off that led to a swoop on the suspects, all women, accused of selling the bouquets in different parts of the capital, Accra. The arrests are the biggest enforcement of the law against misusing the currency. In July, the bank issued a notice warning this could amount to an offence. It warned against "acts that tend to depreciate or impair the national currency, including any conduct that undermines its lawful value or use". Bouquets of banknotes or cakes decorated with currency are often ordered as gifts for weddings, birthdays, graduations and other celebrations. The police have launched investigations, and the authorities say the suspects will be prosecuted. They could face a fine or jail term, to be determined by the court. Dinah Bonzi, an official in the Bank of Ghana's currency department, said anyone aiding or promoting such activities could also be arrested and prosecuted. ''The Ghana cedi is legal tenderâ¦ and must be treated with respect. The misuse or abuse of the currency is an offence and may attract sanctions under the law,'' she said. "Today's arrest should serve as a clear warning to the public. Let us all handle the Ghana cedi with dignity." The central bank has repeatedly warned against activities such as "spraying" - or throwing money at events such as weddings - writing on or altering notes and using them in decorations such as floral-like bouquets in weddings, birthdays and other occasions. The use of money decorations has become more common in Ghana in recent years, with the practice also gaining a foothold in other African countries. In recent years authorities in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Botswana have also issued warnings against misusing the national currencies. Raupelis / LRT Protests over Lithuania's migration policy are taking place in Vilnius on Saturday, with more than 300 people demonstrating against what they call mass immigration. Meanwhile, more than 100 people have gathered for a counter-protest to express their opposition to the demonstration. More than several dozen police vehicles are deployed around Vincas Kudirka Square, near the government building and around the protesters. The demonstrators have been separated by barriers. More than 240 officers are working at the scene to maintain public order, according to ArÅ«nas Paulauskas, the police chief. "We are preparing for any scenario and are ready for it, but we genuinely believe that both rallies, although they are taking place close to one another, will pass with mutual respect and without any major incidents," the commissioner told reporters on Saturday. Concern over scale of immigration The protest in Vincas Kudirka Square is being organised by the far-right National Alliance party. Protesters against migration are holding placards reading "Anti-Lithuanian Inga RuginienÄ, we need neither Islamists nor Filipinos", "We demand an end to the replacement of Lithuanians with foreigners", and others. "Lithuania is a Catholic country, a Christian country, we are very different, [...] we are a Catholic country and it would be very difficult for us to imagine pressure from another religion on our faith," said Laima, a 70-year-old Vilnius resident. Jeronimas RimkÅ«nas, 29, who travelled from Jonava carrying a Lithuanian flag, told BNS that he saw a threat in the scale of immigration. "There is a certain sense of anxiety because I have been following the situation in other European Union countries for quite some time. I have been following the news for about 10 years and, seeing that this wave of migration is gradually reaching our country too, I feel a certain sense of concern," he said. Those attending the protest are demanding stricter deportation of foreigners who commit crimes, the closure of migrant employment centres in foreign countries, known as external service centres, and a reduction in the overall quota for migrants allowed to enter the country. Hundreds protest against migration in Vilnius, more than 100 hold counter-protest | V. Raupelis / LRT Anti-racism protest In response to the National Alliance's initiative, civic activists decided to hold a demonstration against racism at the same time and in the same location, near Vincas Kudirka Square in Vilnius. The demonstration aims to publicly express opposition to the persecution of migrants and other minorities, as well as racist rhetoric. According to the organisers, migrants are increasingly portrayed in the public sphere as a threat to society â being associated with crime, taking jobs or wages, and posing a threat to national security. Gabija, a 26-year-old Vilnius resident who came to oppose the National Alliance's protest, told BNS that the demonstration against migration policy was racist and Islamophobic. "In my value system, belittling people because of their origin, nationality or religious beliefs is simply unacceptable. These are beliefs rooted in violence, which themselves create insecurity when you regard a particular group as lesser people," she said. "The data are being interpreted incorrectly to suggest that they [immigrants] have supposedly increased crime," Gabija said, adding that there is no mass immigration in Lithuania. Laurynas Tomelaitis, 24, one of the organisers of the counter-protest, said he opposed "racism and fascism" and did not see migration as a threat to Lithuania. "Muslims currently make up 1.5% of Lithuania's population. [...] The Muslim community has always been present in Lithuania, so the fact that the National Alliance is against Muslims is, in part, also opposition to Lithuania," he told BNS. Third demonstration in LukiÅ¡kÄs Square Meanwhile, Sienos grupÄ, a public organisation that advocates for migrants' rights, invited people to LukiÅ¡kÄs Square to discuss migration. "Migration is not an ideology or a political programme â it is a social phenomenon that has existed throughout history. People have moved because of war, persecution, work, love, family, studies or simply in search of a better life. Therefore, being generally 'for' or 'against' migration is somewhat like being for or against rain," Sienos grupÄ director Emilija Å vobaitÄ told BNS. According to the Migration Department, 226,999 foreign nationals held residence permits in Lithuania in September. The largest groups were citizens of Ukraine (80,300), Belarus (47,800), Russia (13,200), Uzbekistan (12,600) and India (9,400). LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. Thanks for subscribing! https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: When they bought their 460-acre farm about 30 years ago, the Harrises converted arable fields to pasture. Photograph: Ali Smith/The Guardian View image in fullscreen When they bought their 460-acre farm about 30 years ago, the Harrises converted arable fields to pasture. Photograph: Ali Smith/The Guardian Wetlands ‘You need persistence’: the Norfolk couple who took on environmental regulators three times – and won Tim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk Broads Patrick Barkham Sat 24 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google P olluters and regulators who fail to stop pollution must quake in their boots when they receive a letter from the lawyers for Tim and Geli Harris. The couple, who farm 460 acres in the Norfolk Broads, have now scored a hat-trick of landmark legal victories to save an internationally important wetland after they won again in the high court this month. Lady Justice Lieven found that Natural England failed in its statutory duty to protect Catfield Fen from pollution after nitrates and phosphates washed from arable fields into one of the finest examples of calcareous fen in western Europe, home to 2,500 species including rarities such as the fen orchid, crested buckler fern, breeding bittern and swallowtail butterflies. In a scathing assessment of Natural England’s inaction since the Harrises first reported the pollution to it in 2021, the judge said the cause of the pollution was “the most basic level of common sense” and required action by the government’s conservation watchdog. The Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money taking action to hold to account government agencies for failing to protect the fen, which is part of a special area of conservation (SAC), an internationally important wetland protected by law. The marshes lie within the Broads national park. “This is bigger than a little ditch in Norfolk,” says Tim. He fears that “regulatory inertia” is preventing pollution from being halted on waterways across the country. “Inertia is prevalent throughout all the regulatory bodies. It’s a landmark judgment because it says they can’t just do nothing.” View image in fullscreen Catfield Fen is an internationally important and tremendously diverse wetland. Photograph: Ali Smith/The Guardian The couple are big fans of Dirty Business , the recent Channel 4 dramatisation of a maths professor and a retired detective’s battle against sewage pollution, the water companies and the Environment Agency. “It’s just like that film when you go to a meeting,” Tim says. “The language is from [George Orwell’s] 1984. What we call the light side doesn’t have the money. The dark side does. That’s where the money is. Of course it is.” “They are slippery snakes,” Geli adds. Tim held senior roles in the shipping industry, collecting “the wages of sin”, before turning to environmental campaigning in retirement. “She’s the greenie,” he says of Geli, who grew up near the forests around Heidelberg, Germany, and has always loved the natural world. They bought their farm, which came with a large chunk of Catfield Fen, in 1994, wanting to live closer to nature. They turned their arable fields into pasture to prevent soils and pollution from washing into the fen, and continue to tend English white park cattle, sheep and rare-breed Eriskay ponies. ‘Cash to trash’ levy on house developers too low to offset damage to Norfolk Broads, say critics Read more “It is beautiful,” Geli says of the fen, which requires a careful rotational cut to preserve its rare plants, invertebrates and birdlife. “It’s a little bit of wildness. It’s mysterious. There are places here where we’ve never been – they are pure nature.” Tim says: “It’s taken 1,000 years to create this and people could destroy it very quickly.” Geli adds: “If you water your plants with the wrong water, they die quite quickly.” View image in fullscreen The Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money holding agencies to account for failing to protect the fen. Photograph: Ali Smith/The Guardian The Harrises take conservation advice from the experts at Natural England . “We get on well with Natural England, apart from suing them,” Tim says. “They all came to tea and we talked about everything but the thing [the legal case]. It was a very British occasion. They have some very good people. The trouble is too many no longer have fire in their bellies. They are apparatchiks. We respect them but we wish they had more ‘go’.” Natural England said it accepted the court’s verdict that it had not done enough to protect Catfield Fen but it would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. In 2016, the couple won a public inquiry that demonstrated that too much groundwater was being taken from the valley by water companies and local farmers, causing Catfield Fen to dry out. They won a second battle in 2022 , forcing the Environment Agency to limit the abstraction of water close to other nature-rich sites on the Norfolk Broads. Their principles have cost them local friendships. They say National Farmers’ Union reps rejected their application for membership of the local branch, saying half their members would resign, with farmers upset at restrictions on their abstraction of water to boost lucrative crops such as potatoes. “We’re farmers, we’re not anti-farmer,” Tim says. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Since their 2022 legal victory, the Harrises have noticed an improvement in the water levels and biodiversity of Catfield Fen’s dykes. Geli says: “We are a Noah’s ark until things get better and nature can spread outwards from here again.” View image in fullscreen The couple are campaigning to limit water abstraction in the area. Photograph: Si Barber/The Guardian The fen and its wildlife may be in a better condition under their stewardship, but they are not confident that nature is winning. “The evidence this summer was that the insect numbers are going south, according to the experts who survey here,” Tim says. “We are not complacent; we are very worried.” The judge is to make further rulings on what Natural England must do to stop the pollution of Catfield Fen. For the Harrises, the answer is simple: arable farmers must be paid to put in buffer strips of grassland between their ploughed fields and the ditches leading to the Broads to reduce the nitrate-filled soils washing from arable fields into the fen. View image in fullscreen The couple are considering another legal challenge. Photograph: Si Barber/The Guardian More widely, Tim argues that regulatory bodies must simply put their resources into monitoring and compliance. He fears most breaches of environmental rules go unnoticed because of a lack of both. The Harrises say they do not want to spend their time campaigning. “I don’t want any of this, believe me,” Tim says, gesturing at the box files that take up two walls of shelving. “I’m 79. I want to read books.” He believes the Broads Authority, the government agency responsible for the national park, should be leading the fight against pollution. Nevertheless, they are considering another legal challenge to stop the Broads from being polluted. Their stewardship of Catfield Fen will continue after they go. Their daughter will take on the farm, and she is a lawyer by training. So is their granddaughter. “The agencies are not getting rid of the Harrises when we die,” Tim laughs. Do they hope their example can inspire others to believe they can act to protect nature and clean water? “You need enormous persistence,” Tim says. “You need passion,” Geli adds. “Evil can happen when people do nothing.” Explore more on these topics Wetlands Conservation Natural England Environment Agency Water Environmental activism Farming news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution
